title: EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation becomes applicable
what_happens: PFAS limits on food-contact packaging take effect with no transition period for non-compliant stock; conformity, minimisation and EPR requirements apply to any packaging placed on the EU market. The European Commission's Aug. 1 second-edition FAQ clarified that packaging already produced or in stock before Aug. 12 does not need to be destroyed or relabeled provided it isn't newly placed on the market after that date, and that enforcement will begin with a warning/corrective-action opportunity rather than immediate penalties.
why_watch: Applies regardless of origin, so any EU-bound product or packaging component must comply from this date.
resolution: Became applicable Aug. 12, 2026 as scheduled: PFAS limits on food-contact packaging, conformity/EPR registration and minimisation requirements now apply to any packaging newly placed on the EU market. Per the European Commission's Aug. 1 FAQ, pre-Aug.-12 stock does not need to be destroyed or relabeled, and enforcement begins with a warning/corrective-action step rather than immediate penalties.

title: New York Governor's decision on the GRAS ingredient-disclosure bill
what_happens: Signature or veto due on S.1239F/A.1556G. Legal/trade-press coverage confirms the bill has not yet been formally presented to the Governor; once presented she has 10 days (excluding Sundays) to act, but under NY procedure the Legislature can hold delivery until year-end, giving a statutory backstop of Dec. 31, 2026. No presentment date has been reported yet, so the decision could come at any point between now and then. IDFA has written urging a veto.
why_watch: Would be the first state law mandating disclosure of self-affirmed GRAS safety data, and a likely template for other states.

title: Senate floor action on the Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026
what_happens: Bill advanced out of the Senate HELP Committee 12-10 on July 22, 2026 and awaits a full Senate floor vote; would require front-of-pack warning labels on high sugar, saturated fat and sodium products. UPDATED Sept. 4 scan: no floor vote has occurred as of early September; lawmakers have signaled the bill is likely to see revisions before it comes to the floor, and no new date has been reported. UPDATED Sept. 10 (evening scan): NMPF and IDFA, joined by 76 dairy companies, cooperatives and producer organizations, publicly urged Congress to reject the bill (now referenced in coverage as S. 5026), warning its warning-label thresholds would mischaracterize nutrient-dense dairy foods; no new floor-vote date has been reported.
why_watch: Thresholds would directly implicate whole milk, butter, full-fat cheese and sweetened dairy; the pre-floor-vote window is when positioning matters.

title: Senate Agriculture Committee markup of Farm Bill 2.0 (Agricultural Act of 2026)
what_happens: Committee vote failed 10-11 on Aug. 6 over an unrelated SNAP payment-error-rate dispute (dairy title was not the sticking point). UPDATED Sept. 7 scan: trade-press reporting (Politico Pro, Farm Policy News) now names Sept. 15 specifically — the day after the Senate returns from recess — as the date Chairman Boozman plans to reconvene the committee for the retry vote, tightening this from a 'week of' estimate to a specific day; no formal committee notice has been issued yet and the date could still slip if absent GOP Sens. McConnell or Tuberville are not back. UPDATED Sept. 15 scan: the retry markup has slipped one day — Agri-Pulse now reports the committee is scheduled to reconvene Wednesday, Sept. 16 at 3:30 p.m. ET in the Russell Senate Office Building, not Sept. 15 as earlier reporting indicated. Sen. McConnell is reported returning to work this week after his recovery absence, addressing one of the two attendance risks flagged earlier; Sen. Tuberville's status is unconfirmed.
why_watch: Mandatory dairy-manufacturer cost/yield reporting tied to FMMO pricing, plus reauthorization of the Dairy Indemnity Payment Program and Dairy Promotion and Research Board through 2031, remain pending in the stalled bill.
resolution: Committee reconvened Wednesday, Sept. 16 (one day later than the Sept. 15 date reported earlier in the week) and passed the Agricultural Act of 2026 12-11 along party lines, with Sen. McConnell back on the panel. Sens. Ernst and Grassley objected to the closed amendment process but did not block passage. The dairy title -- reauthorization of the Dairy Forward Pricing Program, Dairy Indemnity Payment Program and Dairy Promotion and Research Board through 2031, plus mandatory dairy-manufacturer cost/yield reporting tied to FMMO pricing -- survived unchanged. Bill advances to the full Senate floor; see companion watch item for the next step.

title: US tariffs on Canadian imports including dairy take effect
what_happens: 50% Section 338 tariffs (signed by proclamation July 20, 2026) on Canadian-origin whey products, milk protein concentrates, lactose, casein/caseinates and milk powders were scheduled to take effect just after midnight Wednesday, Aug. 19; cheese, butter, yogurt, fluid milk/cream, sour cream and ice cream are exempted. UPDATED Aug 19 (early morning scan): Trump announced via Truth Social late Tuesday evening, Aug. 18 — under two hours before the deadline — that the tariffs are paused for three days, citing a deal with Canada "subject to the finalization of documents." PM Carney confirmed the pause, calling it "substantial progress" while cautioning important administrative/documentation work remains before the deal is finalized. The pending deal reportedly involves Canada addressing US concerns on dairy tariff-rate quotas and removing retaliatory bans on US alcohol, among other items. UPDATED Aug 19 (afternoon scan): Trump told reporters he has "come to a deal with Canada" and called it a "very fair deal for both"; Canada's Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said he is "very confident" on the dairy piece specifically, stating "we need to protect supply management" and that "the supply management regime remains entirely intact." UPDATED Aug 19 (later afternoon scan): Multiple outlets (Bloomberg, CP24, CNN) now consistently report the pause runs to end of day Friday, Aug. 21, not Aug. 22 as earlier Axios-sourced reporting suggested; the Aug. 21 date is now treated as the working checkpoint. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette publicly reiterated that dairy supply management is a provincial "red line," underscoring that Canada's political room to concede on dairy market access remains narrow even as both leaders describe the broader deal in positive terms. Deal is not yet finalized; if talks collapse before the checkpoint, the tariffs could still take effect. UPDATED Aug 19 (evening scan): The White House issued a formal proclamation on the pause, stating Canada has expressed commitment to remove measures it considers discriminatory toward US dairy, alcohol and motor-vehicle exports — specifically citing Canada's cheese tariff-rate quotas, which the proclamation says are more restrictive toward the US than the quotas Canada extends to EU cheese. Canada has not yet confirmed those specific commitments. PM Carney is set to brief his cabinet and provincial premiers on the deal, a step read as movement toward finalization but not yet confirmation of final terms. UPDATED Aug 20 (morning scan): US and Canadian trade officials met in person in Washington Aug. 19 to continue negotiating. Trump reiterated the two countries have a deal "subject to the finalization of documents"; Carney used more optimistic language than his Aug. 19 evening comments, saying Canada and the US are "moving towards an agreement" that "reinforces the Canadian advantage." Trade Minister LeBlanc still declined to confirm specific dairy terms, saying talks remain ongoing. No final agreement has been signed as of this scan; the Aug. 21 checkpoint remains the operative date. UPDATED Aug 20 (late-morning scan): New reporting (Bloomberg, Canada's National Observer) says the two sides have reached a negotiated framework: Canada has agreed to Washington's interpretation of how import licenses under Canada's supply-managed dairy sector should be allocated, while Canada's trade minister maintains the underlying supply-management system itself remains "entirely intact." The framework would also roughly halve US tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum (50% to 25%) and cut auto tariffs from 25% to 15%, with Canada dropping retaliatory tariffs and provincial alcohol bans in return. The final legal text is still being completed; the Aug. 21 checkpoint remains the operative date. UPDATED Aug 21 (morning scan): The pause's actual expiry is confirmed by AP-wire and CNBC/CP24 reporting as 12:01 a.m. Saturday, Aug. 22 (not end-of-day Aug. 21 as some earlier reporting suggested). As of Friday morning no final agreement had been signed; officials met in Washington Wed-Thu without completing documents. Trump called the emerging deal "very fair," saying agricultural tariffs on US farmers would go "to zero"; a senior Canadian official called the terms "a very good deal for Canada." PM Carney asked provincial premiers to lift Canada's retaliatory ban on US alcohol sales as a condition of finalizing the deal — Manitoba's premier said there would be no deal without that concession — introducing a new, non-dairy sticking point this close to the deadline. Trade Minister LeBlanc reiterated confidence that dairy supply management specifically remains protected. UPDATED Aug 21 (late-morning scan): LeBlanc and Greer met in person in Washington Friday morning for more than three hours, emerging to call the talks "very close" to a deal; Greer said the two sides have "eliminated some of the irritants" in the relationship. LeBlanc said he is "very confident" specifically on the dairy piece and that Canada's supply-management system will remain in place, but would not say whether its terms would change. No agreement has been signed as of this scan; the Aug. 22 12:01 a.m. checkpoint remains the operative deadline.
why_watch: Whether the pending US-Canada deal is finalized by the Aug. 21 checkpoint determines whether the 50% tariff on Canadian-origin dairy ingredients takes effect at all. Canada's trade minister says supply management is untouched, but a Quebec premier's public red-line comment signals continued domestic political sensitivity on the Canadian side; IDFA and NMPF have both issued public statements urging a swift resolution.
resolution: Talks collapsed just before the extended deadline; PM Carney suspended negotiations the evening of Aug. 21 and recalled Canada's negotiators, vowing to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar.” The 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian-origin whey, milk protein concentrates, lactose, casein/caseinates and milk powders (plus alcohol and autos) took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22 as originally proclaimed; cheese, butter, yogurt, fluid milk/cream, sour cream and ice cream remain exempt. No resumed-talks timeline has been announced.

title: New York Governor's decision on the Food Date Labeling Reform Act
what_happens: A7291B/S7618B passed both houses of the NY Legislature on June 2, 2026 and awaits presentment and the Governor's signature or veto; under NY procedure the Legislature can hold delivery until year-end, giving a statutory backstop of Dec. 31, 2026, with no presentment date yet reported. The bill would replace confusing 'sell by' dates with uniform 'Use By' (safety) and 'Best if Used By' (quality) labels on food produced after July 1, 2028; infant formula and alcoholic beverages are exempted.
why_watch: Would make New York the first state with a uniform two-tier date-labeling standard, a likely template nationally; the 2028 compliance date means packaging and labeling lead-time decisions start well before then.

title: New York Governor's decision on the infant formula/baby food heavy-metal testing and disclosure bill
what_happens: A9026/S8701 passed both houses of the NY Legislature (reported mid-2026) and would require infant formula and baby food manufacturers to test monthly for lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury and publicly disclose results; it awaits presentment and the Governor's signature or veto. As with New York's other pending food bills, the Legislature can hold delivery until year-end, giving a statutory backstop of Dec. 31, 2026; no presentment date has been reported yet. Consumer Reports and state legislators are pushing for a signature, while the infant-formula industry is expected to lobby for a veto. UPDATED Sept. 16 scan: State Sen. Michelle Hinchey publicly cited DOJ's Sept. 14 decision to settle (rather than criminally prosecute) contamination allegations against infant-formula maker Abbott for $385M as new grounds to press Gov. Hochul to sign this bill; no presentment date or gubernatorial action has been reported yet.
why_watch: A third pending New York food-safety/disclosure bill awaiting Hochul's signature alongside the GRAS-disclosure and date-labeling bills; would make New York the first state to mandate heavy-metal testing and disclosure for infant formula, a precedent-setting model for ingredient-safety transparency that trade groups elsewhere would watch closely.

title: FDA's mandatory GRAS-notification proposed rule — Federal Register publication
what_happens: UPDATED: Trade-press and health-policy reporting on Aug. 10 (Food Safety Magazine, STAT News) clarifies the rule (RIN 0910-AJ02) is being filed for Federal Register publication this week — Aug. 11 — not December as earlier reporting anticipated; December was a misread of the comment-period close, not the publication date. Once published it opens a 120-day public comment period (see companion watch item for the close date). HHS Secretary Kennedy publicly announced the proposal Aug. 10, shifting GRAS notification from voluntary to mandatory.
why_watch: Publication starts the comment clock on the biggest change to the GRAS pathway in decades, affecting nearly every food and dairy ingredient supplier that relies on self-affirmed GRAS determinations — four months sooner than the company's tracking assumed.
resolution: Published in the Federal Register Aug. 11, 2026 as scheduled (Document 2026-16296, Docket FDA-2025-N-3262), opening the 120-day comment period.

title: Comment period closes on FDA's mandatory GRAS-notification proposed rule
what_happens: FDA is accepting public comments on the proposed mandatory GRAS-notification rule (RIN 0910-AJ02, Docket FDA-2025-N-3262) for 120 days following its confirmed Aug. 11, 2026 Federal Register publication (Document 2026-16296). Close date calculated from the confirmed 120-day window; watch for the official Federal Register notice text to confirm the exact date.
why_watch: Last opportunity to submit formal comments before FDA can move to finalize the biggest change to the GRAS pathway in decades; ingredient-safety, regulatory and legal teams need lead time to prepare a submission.

title: FDA ultra-processed food definition — outcome of OIRA review
what_happens: FDA/HHS sent a 'Proposed Definition of Ultra-Processed Food' whitepaper to OIRA on August 3, 2026, filed as a notice (not a rule; no legal deadline). On Aug. 10, HHS and USDA publicly confirmed the definition has been submitted for final government review, but its content, and any rule, guidance, or timeline, still has not been released. HHS Secretary Kennedy has said it could become the basis for a front-of-pack red-yellow-green labeling system. UPDATED Aug. 27: pushback continues from multiple directions — food-company CEOs sought a delay earlier in August, and 16 free-market/consumer-rights groups have now separately asked OMB director Russell Vought to block the definition entirely, arguing it lacks scientific grounding and would raise grocery costs. No change to the review's timeline has been reported.
why_watch: Would be the definitional foundation for any future UPF-based labeling or program restriction, running in parallel with the Sanders and Booker/Blumenthal Senate warning-label bills.

title: Public comment period closes on California SB 54's draft EPR program plan
what_happens: Circular Action Alliance's draft statewide Extended Producer Responsibility program plan for SB 54 (California's packaging and plastic EPR law) is open for public comment through August 14, 2026; a final plan is due to CalRecycle in October 2026.
why_watch: SB 54 is the largest state EPR packaging law now in effect; the program plan sets the fee structure and compliance mechanics that determine actual cost to packaged-food manufacturers, and other EPR states are watching California's approach as a template.
resolution: Comment period closed Aug. 14, 2026 as scheduled. Circular Action Alliance will review comments as it prepares the final program plan, due to CalRecycle by October 2026 — that filing is what will actually set the fee structure and compliance mechanics producers face; projected 2027-2031 program costs run $9.3B-$17.2B, funded entirely through producer fees.

title: Douglas, AZ port reopens to Mexican cattle imports under New World screwworm safeguards
what_happens: USDA reopens the Douglas, Arizona port of entry to livestock trade from Mexico under strict New World screwworm inspection protocols on Aug. 24, the first step in a phased reopening; Santa Teresa and Columbus, NM ports would follow if no problems arise. Update Aug. 21: Sonora confirmed its first NWS case on Aug. 19 (a cow ~292 miles from the U.S. border); Sonora released 360,000 sterile flies around the site and stepped up surveillance. USDA said Aug. 21 it has no plans to change the Aug. 24 reopening. Update Aug. 22: AP wire reporting details the phased volume protocol — capped at 700 cattle/day in the reopening's first week, rising to 900/day in week two, and gradually increasing toward 1,300/day thereafter.
why_watch: First reopening of Mexican cattle imports since the border was closed in May 2025 over screwworm; a new detection near the border could reverse the reopening and re-tighten the cattle and dairy-replacement-heifer supply chain.
resolution: Reopening proceeded as scheduled on Aug. 24; the Douglas, AZ port resumed Mexican cattle imports under phased volume caps and screwworm inspection protocols. UPDATE Aug. 27: Sonora's confirmed case count has grown to nine since the initial Aug. 19 detection, with the newest cases near the Chihuahua border roughly 200 miles from the Douglas crossing; USDA has not announced any change to the reopening. Ongoing monitoring warranted for a potential reversal if detections move closer to the border.

title: Ruling expected in Oregon packaging-EPR constitutionality trial (NAW v. Feldon)
what_happens: Following a five-day bench trial in July and post-trial briefs filed July 31, Judge Michael H. Simon skipped oral argument and ordered narrow supplemental briefing (due Aug. 7) on whether the law's small-public-body exemption is facially discriminatory under the Dormant Commerce Clause. A ruling is expected by end of August.
why_watch: First full federal trial testing the constitutionality of a state packaging EPR law; described as a bellwether that could reshape or invalidate elements of EPR programs across all seven states that have enacted them (CA, CO, MD, ME, MN, OR, WA).
resolution: Ruled Aug. 27, 2026: Judge Michael H. Simon upheld Oregon's EPR packaging law, rejecting NAW's Dormant Commerce Clause and Due Process challenges. NAW is expected to appeal to the Ninth Circuit.

title: USDA proposed rulemaking to rewrite bioengineered food disclosure rule
what_happens: A federal court ruled USDA's exemption of highly refined bioengineered ingredients (e.g., refined corn oil, sugar) from mandatory GMO disclosure was arbitrary, and that QR-code-only compliance is unlawful; USDA's Unified Agenda had targeted a proposed rule for August 2026, with the challenged provisions void by Jan. 1, 2028 absent a lawful replacement. UPDATED Aug 31: the August target passed with no NPRM published in the Federal Register; legal-press coverage confirms USDA also missed an earlier July 2026 target for the same rule. No new date has been announced, so this entry uses the following month as a rough placeholder pending USDA's next signal. The parties remain in briefing over the vacatur date for the invalidated digital/text-message disclosure option (plaintiffs want Jan. 1, 2028; USDA wants Jan. 1, 2029), with both sides agreed on Jan. 1, 2028 for the detectability-exemption piece; the district court has not yet ruled on that dispute.
why_watch: Would broaden mandatory bioengineered-ingredient disclosure to more processed foods, including dairy products relying on refined sweeteners or oils, and bar QR-code-only labeling — a compliance approach some manufacturers use.

title: Colorado's response to NAW's preliminary-injunction motion in its packaging-EPR lawsuit
what_happens: The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors sued Colorado (CDPHE) on July 30, 2026 challenging the constitutionality of the Producer Responsibility Program for Statewide Recycling Act (HB 22-1355) on First Amendment (compelled association/dues to Circular Action Alliance) and due-process grounds, and moved Aug. 5 for a preliminary injunction to bar enforcement and defer EPR payment obligations. Colorado's response to that motion was due Sept. 16, 2026. UPDATED Sept. 17 scan: no filing, hearing date or ruling has been reported as of this scan, so the entry now tracks the still-undated next milestone (a ruling on the injunction motion) rather than the passed response deadline.
why_watch: Third state EPR program NAW has challenged after Oregon and California; Oregon's court already granted NAW a partial preliminary injunction, so a similar result in Colorado would extend court-ordered relief from EPR enforcement to a second state ahead of the pending Oregon bellwether ruling (also on this watch list) and add to the litigation risk overhang on all seven EPR states.

title: FDA final rules revoking dairy standards of identity
what_happens: FDA proposed revoking 18 standards of identity for dairy products in July 2025 (RIN 0910-AJ11); the 2026 Unified Regulatory Agenda targets final rules on this and a companion revocation covering other food categories for November 2026.
why_watch: Would remove mandatory compositional/formulation requirements for multiple dairy product categories, giving manufacturers more formulation flexibility while changing the baseline other companies' product and private-label claims are measured against.

title: D.C. Circuit appeal of EPCRA farm air-emissions reporting exemption
what_happens: Environmental groups' appeal of the district court ruling upholding EPA's exemption of factory-farm ammonia/hydrogen sulfide emissions from EPCRA reporting is proceeding before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit; oral arguments expected this fall or possibly not until spring 2027, with no date set yet.
why_watch: A reversal would reinstate EPCRA air-emissions reporting obligations for larger dairy and livestock operations that the industry has spent years litigating to avoid; NMPF and dairy groups are tracking closely.

title: Outcome of PCRM lawsuit seeking withdrawal of the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines
what_happens: Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine sued HHS/USDA in U.S. District Court for D.C. on Aug. 19, 2026, alleging FACA violations in the science-review panel behind the current Dietary Guidelines (eight of nine panelists tied to meat/dairy trade groups, including the National Dairy Council), and asking the court to order the Guidelines withdrawn. Corrected Aug. 23: the date field previously showed the Aug. 19 filing date itself; no hearing or ruling date has been reported, so this is a rough placeholder pending a court schedule, not a predicted ruling date.
why_watch: A ruling ordering withdrawal would remove the Guidelines' current favorable dairy framing (full-fat dairy, whole milk) and keep the industry-influence narrative in the news; watch for a court schedule and for HHS/USDA's response.

title: Canada's promised dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on US goods
what_happens: Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs take effect Sept. 8 on more than 700 US goods worth roughly $20 billion. UPDATED Aug 25: Canada published the full list and rates — dairy and cheese products face 25% duties (steel and aluminum 50%, most other goods 15%), alongside appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp/paper and electronics. PM Carney and Trade Minister LeBlanc confirmed the list; talks collapsed when Washington's final demands "asked too much and offered too little," after Canada had offered to drop remaining steel/aluminum/auto retaliatory tariffs and press provinces to restore US alcohol sales. UPDATED Aug 25 (3pm scan): Trade press (The Western Producer, The Dairy Site) reports the published list breaks the dairy category into two distinct rates, not a flat 25%: milk, cream and dairy ingredients (whey, caseinates, lactose) are hit at 50%, while finished cheese carries the 25% rate. Total value of Canada's package is reported as roughly $20 billion (CNBC) to $27.6 billion (Western Producer) depending on how the U.S. tariffs being mirrored are counted; Canada separately announced a support package for affected workers and businesses worth C$7.5 billion. UPDATED Sept. 7 scan (evening, ET): No pause or delay has been reported; Bloomberg and other wire coverage published today confirm Canada remains on track to impose the tariffs at 12:01 a.m. Sept. 8 as scheduled. PM Carney reiterated in a Sept. 3 interview that Canada is open to resuming talks "when the Americans are ready," pushing back on US Commerce Secretary Lutnick's characterization of the state of negotiations, but no new talks or resumed-negotiation date have been announced.
why_watch: Dairy exposure is uneven, not a flat 25% across the category: ingredient/powder exporters (whey, caseinates, lactose, milk/cream) face the steeper 50% rate, while cheese exporters face 25% — a materially different exposure picture for ingredient-heavy vs. finished-product exporters ahead of the Sept. 8 effective date. UPDATED Aug 24: NMPF and USDEC publicly thanked the Administration for continuing to press Canada and urged a return to the table, while flagging two longer-running USMCA compliance grievances — chronic underfill of Canada's dairy tariff-rate quotas and Canada's use of loopholes on dairy protein exports — that run on a separate track from the Sept. 8 retaliation deadline and could keep this dispute active regardless of how that deadline resolves.
resolution: Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs took effect as scheduled at 12:01 a.m. Sept. 8, 2026: 50% on US milk/cream/dairy ingredients, 25% on finished cheese. No resumed-talks date announced. See 2026-09-08-canada-retaliatory-tariffs-dairy-effective.

title: US Codex Office public meeting on 11th Session of the Codex Committee on Milk and Milk Products
what_happens: USDA/FDA's U.S. Codex Office holds a public meeting to brief stakeholders and take comment on the draft U.S. position ahead of CCMMP11, which then convenes by written correspondence Sept. 29-Oct. 29, 2026.
why_watch: Sets the US negotiating position on international dairy compositional and labeling standards; a formal channel for industry (including individual processors) to weigh in before the US position is finalized.
resolution: Public meeting held via video teleconference as scheduled, 1-3pm ET Sept. 17, 2026, to brief stakeholders and take comment on the draft U.S. position ahead of CCMMP11. As is typical for this kind of stakeholder input session, no substantive readout or outcome has been publicly reported; CCMMP11 itself convenes by written correspondence Sept. 29-Oct. 29, 2026.

title: First round of HHS DEPEND school-nutrition pilot funding awards
what_happens: HHS/AHRQ/NIH expect to make the first round of DEPEND ($32.5M) school-meal pilot funding awards in October, after an application cycle that opens soon.
why_watch: Which pilot approaches and criteria get funded will signal how the administration's 'real food' framing could translate into future school-meal procurement standards.

title: FDA final rule on ultrafiltered/microfiltered milk in standardized cheeses
what_happens: The 2026 Unified Regulatory Agenda (RIN 0910-AI42) targets September 2026 for a final rule amending standards of identity to permit fluid ultrafiltered milk, ultrafiltered nonfat milk, microfiltered milk and microfiltered nonfat milk as ingredients in standardized cheeses and related cheese products, with an exemption from having to separately declare those forms on the label when used alongside milk or nonfat milk. The rulemaking dates to an Oct. 2005 proposal; trade press has flagged the rule as close to release but no publication date has been confirmed yet. UPDATED Sept. 7 scan: no final rule has been published in the Federal Register as of this evening; the September 2026 Unified Agenda target has not yet lapsed, so this remains on track rather than overdue. Watching for publication over the rest of the month. UPDATED Sept. 15 scan: still no final rule published as of mid-September; date moved to Sept. 30 (month-end) since the Unified Agenda target is a monthly estimate, not an exact day.
why_watch: Would give cheesemakers more formulation and sourcing flexibility (using ultrafiltration/microfiltration to standardize protein content) without a labeling change — a direct, decades-pending compliance and cost question for any US cheese manufacturer once finalized.

title: First legal challenge to Section 338 dairy/auto/alcohol tariffs
what_happens: Trade attorneys (Holland & Knight and others) say a lawsuit challenging President Trump's first-ever use of Section 338 tariff authority -- the basis for the 50% tariffs on Canadian dairy ingredients, alcohol and autos -- is expected imminently; none had been filed as of Aug. 29. No court date is set; the listed date is a rough placeholder pending an actual filing. UPDATED Sept. 15 scan: still no lawsuit filed; Liberty Justice Center says it is seeking a plaintiff but has had limited interest so far. Date moved to Sept. 29 as the next likely trigger point (the Canadian dairy/alcohol/motorcycle import ban's effective date), still unconfirmed.
why_watch: A successful challenge could invalidate the Section 338 tariffs on Canadian-origin whey, milk protein concentrates, lactose and casein currently in effect, changing the cost and sourcing picture for ingredient-dependent processors; also relevant to a competing legislative repeal effort (the BAD DEAL Act) introduced Aug. 27.

title: California Governor's decision on the AB 2244 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' food label bill
what_happens: AB 2244 passed the Legislature unanimously (32-0 Senate, 72-0 Assembly) and was sent to Gov. Newsom on Sept. 1, 2026. He has until Sept. 30, 2026 to sign or veto; reporting suggests he is expected to sign.
why_watch: Would create the first state certification seal built around a UPF definition, excluding products with synthetic dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners and certain processing aids — a likely template for other states and a new voluntary labeling distinction touching flavored dairy and processed cheese formulations.

title: Full House Energy & Commerce Committee markup of the PACK Act and Recycled Materials Attribution Act
what_happens: The Commerce, Manufacturing and Trade Subcommittee voice-voted to advance the PACK Act (H.R. 6832) and the Recycled Materials Attribution Act (H.R. 7502) to the full Energy and Commerce Committee on Sept. 1, 2026. No full-committee markup date has been scheduled yet.
why_watch: Would set the next step toward a federal preemption framework for packaging 'recyclable'/'recycled content' claims; environmental advocates are contesting the mass-balance accounting provision as the bills move forward.

title: Comment period on EPA/Army Corps' supplemental WOTUS proposal
what_happens: UPDATED Sept. 9: EPA and the Army Corps' Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (announced Sept. 4) published in the Federal Register Sept. 9, 2026 (Document 2026-18317, 91 FR 57284), seeking further public input on defining "waters of the United States" (WOTUS) under the Clean Water Act, including how to define "relatively permanent" waters and a "continuous surface water connection." Publication confirms the comment deadline as Oct. 9, 2026, replacing the earlier ~Oct. 15 placeholder.
why_watch: WOTUS jurisdiction determines which on-farm and processing-facility waters/wetlands require Clean Water Act permits; the agencies are moving toward a "durable final rule" after roughly 220,000 comments on the original November 2025 proposal, giving dairy/ag stakeholders a fresh, now firmly dated window to weigh in before it is finalized.

title: US import ban on certain Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles takes effect
what_happens: President Trump signed proclamations under Section 338 on Sept. 8, 2026 banning imports of certain Canadian dairy products (including whey), most alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and molasses, citing Canada's continued failure to remove discrimination against US dairy commerce; the ban takes effect three weeks later, on Sept. 29, 2026. It follows Canada's own dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, which took effect Sept. 8. UPDATED Sept. 10 scan: in a national address the evening of Sept. 9, PM Carney called Canada's own retaliatory tariffs necessary to protect Canadian workers and industry but said "I don't believe in escalating the conflict. That's not constructive," and pointed to diversifying trade away from the US rather than signaling further retaliatory measures against the new import ban; no new Canadian counter-action or resumed-talks date has been announced. UPDATED Sept. 10 (evening scan): IDFA issued a statement quantifying exposure — the US imported more than $35 million in whey products from Canada last year — while reiterating support for resolving the underlying dairy trade concerns through negotiation rather than an import ban. UPDATED Sept. 11 (evening scan): Speaking to reporters in Banff at a two-day cabinet retreat, PM Carney said Canada is "still studying" the new import ban and deciding whether to adjust its own retaliatory tariffs in response, characterizing the measures as "relatively modest" compared with earlier US trade actions against Canada — a signal of continued restraint rather than escalation. No new Canadian counter-action, adjustment to Canada's existing retaliatory tariffs, or resumed-talks date has been announced.
why_watch: Would cut off importation of Canadian-origin whey and other dairy ingredients some US processors rely on, adding sourcing risk on top of the existing 50%/25% tariff regime; Carney's Sept. 9 comments read as measured rather than escalatory, but watch for whether that holds or a last-minute negotiated resolution emerges before the Sept. 29 effective date. IDFA's $35M whey-import figure gives a concrete scale reference for the exposure.

title: 50% Section 338 tariff on Canadian specialty cheese and ~70 other goods takes effect
what_happens: As part of the same Sept. 8, 2026 proclamation package that set the Sept. 29 Canadian dairy/alcohol/motorcycle import ban (see companion watch item), the administration also modified the scope of goods already subject to the 50% Section 338 tariff first imposed July 20: roughly 70 additional product categories are added, including specialty cheeses, boats and furniture, effective 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 15, 2026, while a smaller number of items (including rock salt and non-white cement) are removed from the list.
why_watch: Specialty cheese had been exempted from the original July 2026 Section 338 tariffs (which targeted whey, milk protein concentrates, lactose, caseinates and milk powders); this is the first time a finished dairy product — specialty cheese — is added to the 50% tariff, a new and direct cost exposure for anyone sourcing or co-packing Canadian specialty cheese, distinct from the ingredient-tariff and import-ban tracks already on this list.
resolution: Took effect as scheduled at 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 15, 2026: CBP guidance under the Sept. 14 Federal Register proclamation confirms the 50% Section 338 duty now covers Canadian specialty cheeses (cheddar, Swiss, Gruyere, Parmesan, blue-veined and others, under HTSUS headings 9903.03.12 and 9903.03.14) and roughly 70 other goods, while rock salt and cement were removed from the list.

title: California SB 343 'Truth in Recycling' labeling restrictions — scheduled effective date
what_happens: SB 343 would bar the 'chasing arrows' recycling symbol and other recyclability claims on packaging unless a producer can show the material is actually collected and reprocessed by most California recycling programs, with an Oct. 4, 2026 effective date. However, on July 14, 2026 a federal judge (S.D. Cal., California League of Food Producers v. Bonta) granted a preliminary injunction barring the state Attorney General from enforcing the law, finding several provisions likely unconstitutionally vague; California is expected to appeal to the Ninth Circuit. Unless that injunction is stayed or reversed before Oct. 4, the law will not actually take effect as scheduled on that date despite remaining on the books.
why_watch: Would restrict recyclability claims on food and beverage packaging nationally in practice (California is the de facto standard for many national labels), directly affecting dairy tubs, cups and cartons; the pending Ninth Circuit appeal is what will determine whether the Oct. 4 date ends up mattering.

title: 2018 Farm Bill extension (covering dairy support programs) expires
what_happens: The third extension of the 2018 Farm Bill, enacted Nov. 12, 2025 as part of the legislation ending the federal government shutdown, runs through Sept. 30, 2026. The Senate Agriculture Committee's planned Sept. 15 retry markup of Farm Bill 2.0 (Agricultural Act of 2026 — see companion watch item) is the main vehicle in play to enact a full new Farm Bill before the deadline; if that markup fails again or a full bill isn't enacted in time, the remaining 2018-authority programs would need a fourth extension or would lapse to permanent (1949) law. CORRECTION Sept. 11 scan: this entry's original why_watch overstated dairy's stake in the Sept. 30 deadline specifically. Trade-press and CRS/Farm Bureau analysis confirm Dairy Margin Coverage and the Dairy Indemnity Payment Program were already reauthorized through 2031 by the separate One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025 — independent of both the 2018 Farm Bill extension and the still-stalled Farm Bill 2.0 — so neither program lapses on Sept. 30 regardless of the Senate Ag Committee's Sept. 15 markup outcome. What genuinely remains tied to this Sept. 30 deadline is other 2018-authority programs not addressed by OBBBA (e.g., dairy promotion/research board authority status is unconfirmed either way) and the broader farm-safety-net/nutrition titles Farm Bill 2.0 would otherwise replace. UPDATED Sept. 17 scan: with the Senate now expected to recess for the Nov. 3 midterms without a floor vote (see companion senate-farm-bill-floor-vote entry), a full new Farm Bill enacted by Sept. 30 looks increasingly unlikely; a fourth short-term extension of the remaining 2018-authority programs is the more probable outcome, though none has been introduced yet.
why_watch: Distinct from the Sept. 15 committee markup date: whichever 2018-authority dairy and farm-safety-net programs are NOT already covered by OBBBA depend on Farm Bill authority being extended or replaced by Sept. 30 — but per the Sept. 11 correction above, that no longer includes Dairy Margin Coverage or the Dairy Indemnity Payment Program, which are secured through 2031 either way.

title: Full Senate floor vote on Farm Bill 2.0 (Agricultural Act of 2026)
what_happens: Following the Senate Agriculture Committee's 12-11 party-line passage on Sept. 16, 2026, the bill awaits scheduling for a full Senate floor vote. UPDATED Sept. 17 scan: trade press (Farm Policy News/Illinois, DTN) now reports the Senate recesses for the Nov. 3 midterm elections at the end of next week and a floor vote is unlikely before that break; Chairman Boozman has pointed to precedent for passing a farm bill during a post-election lame-duck session. Politico reporting cited in the same coverage flags a real possibility of another short-term extension instead of full Senate passage, given the fragile 12-11 committee margin. Date moved from an early-October placeholder to mid-November to reflect the lame-duck expectation; still unconfirmed.
why_watch: The dairy title's program reauthorizations (through 2031) and new mandatory dairy-manufacturer cost/yield reporting tied to FMMO pricing remain in the bill as it moves to the floor; a slip to lame-duck timing also raises the odds of a further stopgap extension rather than enactment this year (see companion Sept. 30 extension-expiration watch item).

title: Status of Swan v. Rollins dairy-checkoff ESG lawsuit after USDA's funding cutoff
what_happens: Three Wisconsin dairy farmers (represented by the Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty) sued USDA and the National Dairy Promotion and Research Board on June 9, 2026 (E.D. Wis., No. 1:26-cv-01033), arguing mandatory dairy-checkoff assessments were unconstitutionally funding the Innovation Center for U.S. Dairy's ESG/net-zero advocacy. On Sept. 17, 2026 USDA Secretary Rollins directed the National Dairy Board to stop using checkoff funds for ESG/net-zero programs effective immediately (see companion story in today's digest); WILL characterized this as a direct result of the suit, but no source confirms a court order, settlement or dismissal — the case's docket status past the June filing is unconfirmed. No date is set for further proceedings; this entry tracks whatever comes next (a dismissal, a scope dispute, or IDFA/NMPF/DMI's response) with a year-end placeholder pending real developments. UPDATED Sept. 18 scan: the parties have agreed to stay the case while USDA finalizes and implements the checkoff funding change; the lawsuit has not been dismissed, per the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case docket.
why_watch: Whether the case is dismissed as moot, narrows to a scope/compliance dispute over USDA's directive, or continues will determine how durable this week's checkoff funding change is; also watch for the currently-missing public response from IDFA, NMPF and DMI/Innovation Center for U.S. Dairy, which administer the affected programs.

title: Central Valley Regional Water Board revision of dairy waste discharge requirements
what_happens: Following the State Water Resources Control Board's Sept. 15, 2026 statewide order, the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board must revise the region's 2013 dairy general waste discharge requirements to add a 10 mg/L nitrate drinking-water standard, tighter manure storage/land-application rules and alternative drinking-water provisions for affected households. The statewide order sets a five-year outside deadline (by approximately Sept. 2031) for the regional board to finalize those revisions, with phased compliance schedules expected for existing dairies along the way.
why_watch: Sets the compliance timeline and cost exposure for dairy farms across California's Central Valley -- the top US milk-producing region -- that supply a national dairy manufacturer; interim regional board actions and phase-in schedules over the coming years will shape sourcing-region compliance costs well before the outside deadline.
